title: The teacher and the chain
hook: Sufi orders pass teaching from master to student in chains

segments.voice: Yesterday, the turning, sama': listening with the heart, right palm up, left palm down. Your line: receive, give.

A coach takes your wrist, moves it an inch, and suddenly the swing is right. No manual could have told you that inch. A carpenter's apprentice stands beside the bench for years before the cuts come clean. Some knowledge only travels hand to hand. Sufis say the inner path is like that. You can read about it, as al-Ghazali did, but to walk it, the classic Sufi handbooks say, you need a guide who walked it before you, who learned from someone before them, and so on, back and back.
screen: `A COACH MOVES YOUR WRIST AN INCH.` → `SOME THINGS TRAVEL HAND TO HAND.` → `A GUIDE WHO WALKED IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word is silsilah, a chain, like links of metal. In a Sufi order, every teacher, a shaykh, learned from a teacher, who learned from a teacher, all the way back, the Sufis say, to the Prophet ﷺ himself. Students often memorize the names in their chain, and some recite them. Sufi tradition traces chains through 'Ali, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, and the Naqshbandi order is known for its chain through Abu Bakr. Muslims already knew this shape from the hadith. Every hadith comes with an isnad, a chain of narrators: I heard it from so-and-so, who heard it from so-and-so, who heard the Prophet say. Hadith scholars examine each link. The Sufi chain works the same way, but it passes down more than words: a way of practice, and what Sufis call blessing. The link is made by a pledge, bay'ah, often with a handclasp between teacher and student. Sufis connect it to a verse in the Qur'an about the companions who pledged themselves to the Prophet. In Pickthall's words: "The Hand of Allah is above their hands." A chain of hands, one on another, back through the centuries, and above them all, in the Sufis' understanding, God's. There's a warning in the tradition too: a chain is only as good as its links, and Sufi writers themselves warn against false teachers. And a Muslim can learn the faith deeply without joining any order. But for those who take the pledge, their own name becomes the newest link.
screen: `SILSILAH — A CHAIN.` · `BACK TO THE PROPHET, THROUGH 'ALI OR ABU BAKR.` · `LIKE THE ISNAD OF A HADITH.` · `BAY'AH — THE PLEDGE AND THE HANDCLASP.` · then, large: `A CHAIN OF HANDS.`

segments.voice: Think of the people who taught you something that mattered: a parent, a teacher at school, an imam, a coach, a boss, an older friend, and go back one more link if you can: who taught them? Say their names quietly, one by one, like a chain. If you pray, you can pray for every name on your chain.
Silsilah. The chain of teachers in a Sufi order, reaching back, hand to hand, toward the Prophet. Today's word.
Your line: a chain of hands. Every teacher once learned from a teacher. Day three hundred three, done.

howItsDone: Members of Sufi orders take a pledge, bay'ah, with a living shaykh and learn the practices of their order's chain; some recite the names of their chain, while other Muslims learn the faith from scholars and teachers without joining an order.

fork.setup: you want to walk the Sufi path, not just read about it. what do the Sufi handbooks say you need?
options: a guide, in a chain of teachers, who walked it before you.
